section_1a.directions: Section I, Part A — Multiple Choice: 55 questions, 55 minutes. Each question is followed by four answer choices. Select the choice that best answers the question or completes the statement. This part counts for 40 percent of the exam score. Work briskly; all questions count equally.

items.stem: Prescott's work belongs to which historiographical tradition?

stimulus.text:
Questions 33–36 refer to the following excerpt.

The historian portrays Cortés as a daring and resourceful commander whose small Spanish force toppled the Aztec Empire through bold leadership, shrewd alliances with peoples subject to the Aztecs, and superior weaponry — while also recording the cruelty of the conquest.
—After William H. Prescott, History of the Conquest of Mexico, 1843 (paraphrased)

options: A. Marxist social history focused on class struggle
B. The Annales school's long-durée structural history
C. Nineteenth-century narrative history of great men and events
D. Quantitative cliometrics and statistical analysis
items.explanation: Prescott wrote in 1843, and his book is a dramatic narrative built around Cortés — a daring leader — and the fall of the Aztec Empire. That is the hallmark of nineteenth-century narrative history: vivid storytelling about great men and decisive events, written before professional historians adopted social-science methods. The excerpt focuses on leadership, alliances, and battlefield outcomes, not on structures or statistics.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Marxist social history explains events through class struggle and material conditions; Prescott explains the conquest through a commander's boldness and alliances, not through economic classes.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Annales school is a twentieth-century French movement that studies long-term structures and slow change; Prescott wrote a century earlier about a single dramatic campaign.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The passage is a nineteenth-century narrative of great men and events: it centers on Cortés's daring leadership and the decisive toppling of an empire, which is exactly how historians of Prescott's era wrote history.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Cliometrics is twentieth-century quantitative history built on statistics; Prescott offers a narrative of personalities and events, not data analysis.

items.stem: Which of the following did NOT help drive European expansion into the Western Hemisphere? The engraving above, Theodor de Bry's 1594 depiction of Columbus's landing on Hispaniola, illustrates the European expansion the question asks about.

stimulus.image_caption: Theodor de Bry, 'Columbus landing on Hispaniola,' 1594 — Spanish claim-taking in the Caribbean.
stimulus.pd_rationale: Theodor de Bry, 1594; pre-1930 publication

options: A. Pursuit of wealth and new markets
B. The spread of Christianity
C. The rise of democratic government in Europe
D. Advances in ships and navigation
items.explanation: Europe's push into the Western Hemisphere was driven by the search for wealth and new markets, the desire to spread Christianity, and new ships and navigation tools such as the caravel, the compass, and better charts. Democratic government played no role: fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Europe was ruled by monarchs, and democratic movements came centuries later. The engraving of Columbus's landing illustrates an age of monarchy-sponsored exploration, not democracy.

option_explanations.A: This did help drive expansion, so it is not the answer. The search for gold, spices, and new trade routes was a central motive for voyages like Columbus's.
option_explanations.B: This did help drive expansion, so it is not the answer. Spreading Catholicism was an explicit goal of Spanish and Portuguese exploration.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this did NOT help drive expansion. Europe in the 1400s and 1500s was governed by kings and queens, not democracies; democratic government expanded much later and had nothing to do with launching overseas exploration.
option_explanations.D: This did help drive expansion, so it is not the answer. Advances in shipbuilding and navigation made long ocean voyages possible for the first time.

items.stem: The ideas represented in the excerpt above were most reflected in American policy in the 20th century through

stimulus.text: Source 1: “He who is by nature not his own but another’s man, is by nature a slave; and he may be said to be another’s man who, being a human being, is also a possession.” Source: Aristotle, Politics, Book I (c. 350 BCE; Benjamin Jowett translation, 1885 — public domain). Source 2: Paraphrased from Mary Ann Glendon, “The Forgotten Crucible: The Latin American Influence on the Universal Human Rights Idea” (2003). Glendon argues that as Latin American nations gained independence in the nineteenth century, two intellectual strains merged with an older, more universalist natural-law tradition to produce a distinctively Latin American discourse of rights. She traces its roots to the Spanish Dominicans — above all Bartolomé de Las Casas, the sixteenth-century bishop who condemned slavery and defended Native peoples on the basis of a natural right to liberty grounded in a single common humanity: “All the peoples of the world are humans,” Las Casas wrote, “and all the races of humankind are one.” Following Paolo Carozza and Brian Tierney, Glendon credits Las Casas and his fellow Dominicans with laying the groundwork for a doctrine of natural rights independent of religious revelation, drawn instead from human rationality and free will and from Aristotelian philosophy.

options: (A) Moral Imperialism
(B) Cold War politics
(C) the Good Neighbor Policy
(D) free trade agreements like NAFTA
items.explanation: The excerpt traces a Latin American tradition of universal human rights back to Las Casas, who defended Native peoples on the ground of a single common humanity and a natural right to liberty. In the twentieth century, that spirit appeared in U.S. policy as the Good Neighbor Policy: Franklin Roosevelt's 1930s pledge to respect Latin American sovereignty, renounce armed intervention, and deal with neighbors as equals rather than subjects.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Moral imperialism — associated with Woodrow Wilson's interventions in places like Mexico and Haiti — imposed American values by force, the opposite of respecting a shared humanity.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Cold War policy toward Latin America was driven by anti-communism and often supported coups against elected governments, not by the universal-rights tradition described here.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Good Neighbor Policy embodied the excerpt's idea: treating Latin American nations as fellow members of one human community entitled to liberty and non-intervention.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. NAFTA was a 1990s agreement about tariffs and trade, not an expression of the human-rights philosophy in the excerpt.

items.stem: The speaker above would be most associated with which of the following social or political movements?

stimulus.image_caption: George Whitefield preaching to a crowd (engraving, 1857).
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1857 engraving; pre-1930
stimulus.text_stimulus: “As for the lawfulness of keeping slaves, I have no doubt, since I hear of some that were bought with Abraham’s money, and some that were born in his house.—And I cannot help thinking, that some of those servants mentioned by the Apostles in their epistles, were or had been slaves. It is plain, that the Gibeonites were doomed to perpetual slavery, and though liberty is a sweet thing to such as are born free, yet to those who never knew the sweets of it, slavery perhaps may not be so irksome.” Source: George Whitefield, 1751

options: (A) Republicanism
(B) Abolitionism
(C) The Age of Reason
(D) The First Great Awakening
items.explanation: The speaker is an emotional revival preacher of the sort that defined the First Great Awakening of the 1730s and 1740s. Itinerant ministers like George Whitefield drew huge outdoor crowds with dramatic sermons calling listeners to a personal, heartfelt conversion experience. That style of passionate, mass religious revival is the movement's signature.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Republicanism is the Revolutionary-era political ideology of civic virtue and resistance to tyranny, not a religious preaching movement.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Abolitionism was the nineteenth-century movement to end slavery, a century after this speaker's era.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Age of Reason celebrated Enlightenment rationality and was skeptical of religious enthusiasm — the opposite of a revival sermon.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The speaker's fervent revival preaching matches the First Great Awakening, when traveling ministers sparked mass conversions across the colonies.

items.stem: Josephe's testimony indicates that the Pueblo rebels did which of the following?
options: (A) The rebels had been so thoroughly Christianized that their uprising was purely an economic protest.
(B) The rebels limited themselves to peaceful, nonviolent forms of protest against Spanish rule.
(C) The rebels attacked Spanish religious and cultural symbols as well as the colonial labor system.
(D) The rebels traded freely with the Spanish and rebelled only against new taxes on that trade.
items.explanation: Josephe's testimony describes the Pueblo Revolt of 1680 as a wholesale rejection of Spanish rule. The rebels killed missionaries and settlers, burned churches, destroyed Christian images, and threw off the encomienda system of forced Indian labor. It was not a narrow protest: it attacked both the Catholic religious order the Spanish had imposed and the labor system that exploited Pueblo people.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The revolt was not purely economic. The rebels deliberately destroyed churches and killed priests, showing they were rejecting Spanish Christianity and culture as well as labor demands.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The revolt was violent — hundreds of Spaniards were killed and Santa Fe was besieged — not a campaign of peaceful nonviolent protest.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Josephe's account shows the rebels striking at Spanish religious and cultural symbols (churches, priests, Christian images) and at the colonial forced-labor system together.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The rebels were not protesting a new tax on trade; they rose up to expel the Spanish entirely and restore Pueblo religious and community life.

items.stem: De Bry's engraving is best understood as an expression of which of the following?

stimulus.image_caption: Theodor de Bry, 'The Natives of Florida Worship the Column Erected by the Commander on His First Voyage,' Grand Voyages, 1591 (Library of Congress).
stimulus.pd_rationale: Theodor de Bry after Jacques Le Moyne, 1591; Library of Congress, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 5-8 refer to the image above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: (A) {'letter': 'A', 'text': 'European fear of native peoples'}
(B) {'letter': 'B', 'text': 'European religious fervor'}
(C) {'letter': 'C', 'text': 'European doubts about the value of exploration'}
(D) {'letter': 'D', 'text': 'European curiosity about the wider world'}
items.explanation: Theodor de Bry never crossed the Atlantic; he produced his engravings in Europe for readers hungry for news of the New World. His detailed, dramatic images of Columbus's landing fed that appetite, presenting the encounter as a marvel of discovery. The engraving is best read as a product of Europe's fascination with the wider world it was just beginning to explore.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The engraving dramatizes the landing as a moment of discovery and wonder; it does not present native peoples as a source of fear.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The image's emphasis is on the encounter with a new land and its peoples, not on missionary zeal or religious devotion.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Nothing in the engraving questions whether exploration was worthwhile — it celebrates the arrival.
option_explanations.D: Correct. De Bry's engraving catered to European curiosity about the Americas, picturing the landing as an exciting first contact with an unknown world.

items.stem: The act's requirement that colonial goods be carried only in English ships was intended to

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"For the increase of shipping and encouragement of the navigation of this nation, wherein, under the good providence and protection of God, the wealth, safety, and strength of this kingdom is so much concerned... no goods or commodities whatsoever shall be imported into or exported out of any lands... belonging to his Majesty... but in such ships as do truly and without fraud belong only to the people of England..."
—Navigation Act of 1660 (abridged)

options: A. Open colonial ports to the ships of all nations
B. Enrich English merchants and shipbuilders by excluding Dutch competitors
C. Lower the prices colonial consumers paid for imported goods
D. Encourage manufacturing industries within the colonies
items.explanation: The Navigation Act of 1660 ordered that goods shipped to and from the colonies travel only on English vessels. The purpose was mercantilist: to build English shipping and merchant wealth while shutting out the Dutch, who then dominated the carrying trade. England wanted the profits of colonial commerce to flow to English merchants and shipbuilders, not to foreign competitors.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The act did the opposite of opening trade — it closed colonial ports to foreign ships and reserved the carrying trade for England.
option_explanations.B: Correct. By requiring English ships, the act funneled shipping profits to English merchants and shipbuilders and cut the Dutch out of the colonial trade they had dominated.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Restricting who could carry goods reduced competition, which tended to raise prices for colonial buyers rather than lower them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Navigation Acts discouraged colonial manufacturing; the colonies were meant to supply raw materials and buy finished goods from England.

items.stem: In the context of the letter, Washington's remark that Americans 'had too good an opinion of human nature' most nearly means which of the following?
options: (A) Deist theology had wrongly discarded the Calvinist doctrine of original sin.
(B) Americans had naively trusted Britain to honor the Treaty of Paris (1783).
(C) The army had misjudged the willingness of Ohio Valley tribes to live peacefully alongside white settlers.
(D) The Articles' framers trusted too much in voluntary cooperation and gave Congress no coercive power.
items.explanation: Washington wrote this during the Confederation period, when Congress had no power to tax, no power to compel the states, and no executive to enforce its will. His remark means the Articles of Confederation were designed on the naive hope that the states would cooperate voluntarily out of goodwill. Experience proved otherwise — states ignored requisitions — which is why Washington concluded a stronger national government was necessary.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Washington is making a practical political criticism of the Articles' design, not a theological argument about Calvinist doctrine.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The letter concerns the weakness of the Confederation government, not diplomacy with Britain after the 1783 treaty.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Frontier relations with Ohio Valley tribes were a real concern, but this remark targets the structure of American government, not Indian policy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Washington means the Articles' framers trusted too much in voluntary state cooperation and gave Congress no power to compel it.

items.stem: [Image description: a 1767 political cartoon by Benjamin Franklin, 'Magna Britannia: Her Colonies Reduc'd.' A dismembered female figure of Britannia lies fallen from a globe, her severed limbs labeled with the names of North American colonies; British merchant ships sit idle in the background; a rejected olive branch lies on the ground; a banner across her body reads 'Date Obolum Bellisario' — 'give a farthing to Belisarius,' the Roman general reduced to begging.] What is the cartoon's central warning?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The Colonies Reduc'd' (companion to Franklin's 'Magna Britannia: Her Colonies Reduc'd'), after Benjamin Franklin, published 1768 — the severed limbs of the empire, labeled with colony names.
stimulus.pd_rationale: After Benjamin Franklin, published by John Almon, 1768; British Museum, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The cartoon above (replacing the bracketed description): the companion to Franklin's 'Magna Britannia: Her Colonies Reduc'd,' showing the severed limbs of the empire labeled with colony names.

options: (A) The thirteen colonies should unite to press their grievances more forcefully against Britain.
(B) The colonists needed stronger militias to defend themselves against British attack after 1763.
(C) British tax policies risked crippling — even dismembering — the British Empire itself.
(D) A British standing army in America would inevitably destroy colonial liberties.
items.explanation: Franklin's cartoon shows Britannia dismembered, her severed limbs labeled with the names of the colonies — a stark visual warning to Parliament. His point was that tax policies meant to squeeze revenue from America were tearing the empire itself apart. By alienating the colonies, Britain risked destroying the imperial unity and prosperity those policies were supposed to serve.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon warns Britain about the consequences of its own policies; it is not a call for the colonies to unite (that was Franklin's earlier Join, or Die).
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The cartoon is about taxation and imperial unity, not about building colonial militias for defense.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The dismembered Britannia warns that British tax policies were crippling — literally cutting apart — the empire itself.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. A standing army is not the cartoon's subject; the severed limbs represent the colonies being cut away by fiscal policy.

items.stem: Unlike many later patriots, Dickinson's argument in the Letters stopped short of independence because he

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

options: A. believed Parliament had a right to tax the colonies
B. He still hoped for reconciliation with Britain within the empire
C. He feared an invasion by France
D. He served as a royal official in Pennsylvania
items.explanation: Dickinson's Letters argued that Parliament had no right to tax the colonies, but he stopped short of calling for independence because he still believed the empire could be set right. He was a loyal British subject who wanted the colonies' rights restored within the imperial system, not a break from it. His resistance aimed at reconciliation on fair terms, not revolution.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Dickinson explicitly denied Parliament's right to tax the colonies; what he rejected was independence, not the argument against taxation.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Dickinson still hoped for reconciliation with Britain inside the empire, so his argument pressed for restored rights rather than a complete break.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Fear of a French invasion was not what restrained him; his restraint came from loyalty to the empire and hope it could be reformed.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Dickinson was a colonial lawyer and pamphleteer, not a royal official.

items.stem: The cartoon above supports which one of the following conclusions?

stimulus.image_caption: 'The savages let loose, or The cruel fate of the Loyalists,' British cartoon, 1783 (Library of Congress) — three figures representing America murdering Loyalists.
stimulus.pd_rationale: 1783; Library of Congress British Cartoon Prints Collection, pre-1930
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: The cartoon above (replacing the bracketed description): 'The savages let loose, or The cruel fate of the Loyalists' (1783).

options: (A) After the British victory in the Seven Years’ War, many Native Americans sought revenge on British aristocrats.
(B) The French withdrawal from North America after the Seven Years’ War led to various conflicts between Native Americans and colonial settlers.
(C) During and after the Revolutionary War, American sentiment toward those loyal to Britain became increasingly hostile.
(D) Native American warriors were eager to fight alongside American patriots during the American Revolution.
items.explanation: The cartoon depicts the harsh American treatment of Loyalists during and after the Revolution — the period when neighbors who sided with Britain faced boycotts, tarring and feathering, confiscation of property, and exile. It reflects how patriot sentiment hardened: loyalty to the Crown came to be seen as betrayal, and Loyalists were driven out of communities they had lived in for years.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon concerns the Revolutionary era and American hostility toward Loyalists, not Native American revenge after the Seven Years' War.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The subject is American attitudes toward Britain's supporters, not conflicts between Native Americans and settlers after the French withdrawal.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The cartoon shows that during and after the Revolution, American feeling toward those loyal to Britain turned increasingly hostile.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The cartoon portrays hostility toward Loyalists, not Native warriors fighting alongside the patriots.

items.stem: Dickinson's argument in the passage most directly continues which earlier colonial tradition?

stimulus.text:
The following questions refer to the excerpt below.

"A perpetual jealousy, respecting liberty, is absolutely requisite in all free states. The very texture of their constitution, in mixed government, demands it... Let us take care of our rights, and we therein take care of our prosperity."
—John Dickinson, Letters from a Farmer in Pennsylvania, 1767–1768 (abridged)

options: A. The divine-right theory of monarchy
B. The mercantilist defense of imperial trade regulation
C. The colonial claim to the traditional rights of Englishmen
D. The Great Awakening's evangelical individualism
items.explanation: Dickinson's call for perpetual jealousy in defense of liberty belongs to the long colonial tradition of claiming the traditional rights of Englishmen. For over a century, colonists had argued they carried English liberties with them — no taxation without representation, trial by jury, government by consent — and Dickinson's Letters extend that argument against Parliament's new taxes. He frames resistance as the defense of inherited English rights, not as a new invention.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Divine-right theory justifies absolute monarchy; Dickinson argues the opposite — that free people must jealously guard their liberty.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Mercantilism defends imperial control of trade; Dickinson is defending colonial rights against that very system.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Dickinson's argument continues the colonial claim to the traditional rights of Englishmen, insisting Americans possessed the same liberties as subjects in Britain.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Great Awakening was a religious revival about personal conversion, not a tradition of constitutional argument about English rights.

items.stem: This cartoon criticizes which Jefferson policy?

stimulus.image_caption: 'Ograbme, or the American Snapping-Turtle,' embargo cartoon, 1807.
stimulus.stimulus_replacement: Questions 1-4 refer to the cartoon above (replacing the bracketed description).

options: A. The War with Tripoli
B. The Louisiana Purchase
C. The Embargo Act
D. Reductions in federal spending
items.explanation: The cartoon mocks the Embargo Act of 1807, Jefferson's attempt to punish Britain and France by halting American trade with the world. The embargo devastated American merchants, sailors, and farmers while failing to change European behavior, and it became a favorite target of Federalist cartoonists. Jefferson's policy hurt Americans far more than it hurt the intended targets.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The war with Tripoli (1801–1805) was a naval conflict with Barbary pirates, not the subject of this cartoon's criticism.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Louisiana Purchase was widely popular and doubled the nation's size; it was not a target of this mockery.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The cartoon criticizes Jefferson's Embargo Act, which shut down American foreign trade and inflicted severe economic pain at home.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Cuts in federal spending were not the controversial policy being satirized; the embargo's trade shutdown was.

items.stem: Washington's Farewell Address was written most directly in response to which of the following?

stimulus.text: "Observe good faith and justice towards all nations; cultivate peace and harmony with all.... The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible.... Europe has a set of primary interests which to us have none; or a very remote relation." — President George Washington, Farewell Address, 1796

options: (A) The British burning of Washington, D.C.
(B) The outbreak of the Mexican-American War.
(C) Bitter partisan divisions between Federalists and Democratic-Republicans and the pull of the Anglo-French war on American loyalties.
(D) South Carolina's nullification of the tariff.
items.explanation: By 1796, Americans had split into bitterly opposed Federalists and Democratic-Republicans, largely over whether to favor Britain or revolutionary France in the Anglo-French war. Washington watched partisanship tear at national unity and wrote the Farewell Address to warn against permanent foreign alliances and the spirit of party. The address was his direct answer to a republic dividing itself along foreign-policy lines.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The British burned Washington in 1814, eighteen years after the Farewell Address was written.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Mexican-American War began in 1846, half a century after 1796.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Washington wrote most directly against the bitter Federalist versus Democratic-Republican split and the way the Anglo-French war was pulling American loyalties apart.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. South Carolina's nullification of the tariff was an 1830s crisis, decades after the Farewell Address.

items.stem: The American colonists objected to the policies imposed by Parliament after the French and Indian War for all of the following reasons EXCEPT
options: (A) the new restrictions would hinder New England trade
(B) their rights as Englishmen were being violated
(C) they resented quartering British troops now that the French threat was removed
(D) they wanted colonial representatives seated in Parliament in London
items.explanation: After the French and Indian War, colonists protested Parliament's taxes and trade restrictions, defended their rights as Englishmen, and resented quartering troops now that the French threat was gone. What they did not do was ask for seats in Parliament. Their argument was that Parliament had no authority to tax them at all — sending a few colonial delegates across the Atlantic would not have fixed what they saw as a violation of their rights.

option_explanations.A: Colonists did object on these grounds, so this is not the answer. New trade restrictions like the Sugar Act threatened New England merchants' livelihoods.
option_explanations.B: Colonists did object on these grounds, so this is not the answer. They argued that being taxed by a body in which they had no voice violated their rights as Englishmen.
option_explanations.C: Colonists did object on these grounds, so this is not the answer. With the French defeated, they saw no reason to house British soldiers in peacetime.
option_explanations.D: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Colonists never demanded seats in Parliament; they argued Parliament lacked the authority to tax them entirely, and a handful of distant representatives would not have answered that objection.

items.stem: Ames's attack on 'the American jacobin party' identifies him with which of the following?

stimulus.text: "Did [this treaty] not . . . annex Louisiana, and squander millions in a week? . . . The American jacobin party, by rousing the popular passions, inevitably augments the powers of government, and contracts within narrower bounds . . . the privileges of the people. . . . What limits are there to the prerogatives of the present administration? . . . The Constitution, alas! that sleeps with Washington . . ." — Fisher Ames, Federalist congressman from Massachusetts, letter on the Louisiana Purchase treaty, 1803

options: (A) The Whigs.
(B) The Democratic-Republicans.
(C) The Anti-Federalists of the ratification era.
(D) The Federalists.
items.explanation: Fisher Ames was a leading Federalist congressman from Massachusetts, and jacobin was the Federalists' insult for Thomas Jefferson's Democratic-Republicans, whom they painted as dangerous French-style radicals. Ames is attacking Jefferson's party for rousing popular passions and stretching executive power — classic Federalist rhetoric. The Louisiana Purchase, which he also denounces, was Jefferson's achievement.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Whigs were a later party of the 1830s–1850s, formed in opposition to Andrew Jackson — not Ames's party in 1803.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Democratic-Republicans were the very party Ames is attacking as the American jacobin party.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Anti-Federalists opposed the Constitution in the 1780s; by 1803 Ames was defending strong national government, the opposite position.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Ames's attack on the jacobin party and his defense of constitutional limits identify him as a Federalist.

items.stem: The style of campaigning satirized in the passage was made necessary primarily by which of the following?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1840 (campaign lithograph; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus: "When the day of election approaches, visit your constituents far and wide. Treat liberally, and drink freely, in order to rise in their estimation.... Do all you can to appear to advantage in the eyes of the women.... kiss and slabber their children, wipe their noses, and pat them on the head.... Promise all that is asked... Offer to build a bridge or a church... Promises cost nothing.... Get up on all occasions... and make long-winded speeches.... Talk of your devotion to country, your modesty and disinterestedness.... Rail against taxes of all kinds, officeholders, and bad harvest weather." — Robert Penn Smith (as David Crockett), Colonel Crockett's Exploits and Adventures in Texas, 1837

options: (A) The rise of national party nominating conventions.
(B) The elimination of property qualifications for voting, which vastly expanded the electorate.
(C) The invention of the electric telegraph.
(D) The introduction of federal funding for political campaigns.
items.explanation: The satirized campaigning style — mass rallies, parades, slogans, and treating voters — belongs to the Jacksonian era, when states began dropping property requirements for voting. Suddenly hundreds of thousands of ordinary white men could vote, and candidates had to appeal to a mass electorate rather than a small circle of property holders. Popular campaigning became necessary because the voters candidates needed to persuade had enormously multiplied.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. National nominating conventions did develop in this era, but they organized party leadership; the mass campaign style was driven by the need to reach vastly more voters.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Eliminating property qualifications hugely expanded the electorate, forcing candidates to campaign to the masses with rallies, slogans, and spectacle.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The telegraph (1840s) came later than the Jacksonian campaign revolution of the 1820s–1830s.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Federal funding of campaigns did not exist in this era; campaigns were financed privately and by parties.

items.stem: The Pennsylvania law and its enforcement reflected an ongoing conflict between which of the following?
options: (A) Rural and urban interests.
(B) Federal law and state law.
(C) Gradual-emancipation and immediate-emancipation advocates.
(D) Supporters and opponents of federal commerce regulation.
items.explanation: The Pennsylvania law — a personal-liberty law meant to protect free Black residents from kidnapping — collided with federal fugitive-slave legislation, which required the return of people claimed as runaways. When state law and federal law commanded opposite outcomes, the conflict exposed the unresolved question of which level of government prevailed. The enforcement struggle was a federal-versus-state clash, not a dispute within one level.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The conflict was not between rural and urban interests but between two levels of government giving contradictory commands.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Pennsylvania's law and its enforcement clashed with federal law, making this a federal-versus-state conflict over whose authority governed.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The dispute was about the collision of state and federal law, not a debate between gradual and immediate emancipation strategies.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Federal commerce regulation was not at issue; the conflict concerned personal liberty and fugitive-slave enforcement.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes a change in westward migration in the 1840s?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Painted 1851 by Arthur Nahl. Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: (A) The number of pioneers headed for the Oregon Territory decreased while the number headed for California greatly increased.
(B) The first great wave of migration ended, and the number of migrants remained extremely low until after the Civil War.
(C) For the first time, pioneers began to settle areas west of the Mississippi River.
(D) Large numbers of free Black people, unwelcome in the East, began to resettle in the West.
items.explanation: In the early 1840s, most overland migrants headed for the Oregon Territory. The discovery of gold in California in 1848–1849 transformed the pattern: migration to Oregon fell off while tens of thousands of forty-niners rushed to California instead. The Gold Rush redirected the great westward movement from the Pacific Northwest to California within just a few years.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Oregon-bound migration declined in the late 1840s while California-bound migration exploded after the gold discovery.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Migration did not end or stay low — the Gold Rush produced one of the largest migrations in American history.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Pioneers had been settling west of the Mississippi since long before the 1840s, including in Texas and Oregon.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The great movement of free Black settlers westward came later, especially the Exoduster movement to Kansas in the late 1870s.

items.stem: The Free-Soil Party advocated which of the following?
options: (A) The freedom of settlers within the territories to determine the slave status of their new state
(B) The passage of the Homestead Act to give free land to all Western settlers
(C) The exclusion of slavery from any of the new territories
(D) The policy of giving newly freed enslaved people “40 acres and a mule” following the Civil War
items.explanation: The Free-Soil Party, founded in 1848, organized around one central principle: slavery must not be allowed to spread into the western territories. Its slogan was free soil, free labor, free men — the idea that the territories should be reserved for free white labor rather than slave labor. The party did not demand immediate abolition where slavery already existed; its fight was about keeping slavery out of new lands.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Letting settlers decide slavery's status was popular sovereignty, the Democratic position — not the Free-Soil demand to ban slavery from the territories outright.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Homestead Act (1862) came later, during the Civil War, and was not the Free-Soil Party's platform.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Free-Soil Party's core demand was excluding slavery from all new territories.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Forty acres and a mule was a Reconstruction-era proposal for freedpeople after the Civil War, not a Free-Soil position.

items.stem: This political cartoon of Andrew Jackson was least likely to have been sketched by a supporter of which of the following political parties?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1832, artist unknown (Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed on Commons file page (observed 2026-10-01).
stimulus.text_stimulus: King Andrew the First , Unknown Artist, c. 1833

options: (A) Whig
(B) National Republican
(C) Anti-Masonic
(D) Democratic
items.explanation: Andrew Jackson was the founder and hero of the Democratic Party, so a hostile cartoon mocking him would not come from his own supporters. The Whigs, National Republicans, and Anti-Masons all opposed Jackson and produced savage anti-Jackson imagery — portraying him as a would-be king or tyrant. A Democratic supporter would have had no reason to sketch an attack on their own party's leader.

option_explanations.A: A Whig opponent could easily have sketched this — the Whigs defined themselves against Jackson's executive power.
option_explanations.B: A National Republican opponent could easily have sketched this — they were Jackson's rivals in the elections of 1824 and 1828.
option_explanations.C: An Anti-Masonic opponent could easily have sketched this — the party opposed Jackson, who was a prominent Mason.
option_explanations.D: Correct — least likely. Jackson founded the Democratic Party; his own supporters would not circulate a cartoon attacking him.

items.stem: The Hartford Convention demonstrated that
options: A. The Federalist Party remained nationally dominant
B. The War of 1812 unified American politics
C. Nullification was not an exclusively Southern doctrine
D. The Treaty of Ghent deeply divided the country
items.explanation: The Hartford Convention of 1814–1815 was a gathering of New England Federalists, furious at the War of 1812 and the embargoes, who discussed resistance to federal policy — including talk of nullification and even secession. That is the significance: nullification, the doctrine of states blocking federal law, was being championed by Northern Federalists decades before Southern states used it. It was never an exclusively Southern idea.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The convention actually hastened the Federalist Party's collapse — it was branded as disloyal once the war ended.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The convention showed deep division, not unity; New England Federalists were protesting a war the rest of the country supported.
option_explanations.C: Correct. New England Federalists at Hartford embraced nullification talk, proving the doctrine was not exclusively Southern.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Treaty of Ghent ended the war and undercut the convention; it did not divide the country the way the war itself had.

items.stem: Andrew Johnson was impeached because
options: (A) he refused to carry out Lincoln’s plan for reconstruction
(B) he vetoed the Wade-Davis Bill
(C) Congress was controlled by Republicans and he was a Democrat
(D) he violated the Tenure of Office Act by firing Secretary of War Stanton
items.explanation: Congress passed the Tenure of Office Act in 1867 to prevent President Andrew Johnson from removing officials without Senate approval. Johnson deliberately defied it by firing Secretary of War Edwin Stanton, a Radical Republican ally, daring Congress to act. The House impeached him for that violation — the legal charge on which the whole case rested.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Johnson had his own lenient Reconstruction plan; the impeachment charge was the specific legal violation, not his general refusal to follow Lincoln's approach.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Wade-Davis Bill was a wartime 1864 measure that Lincoln pocket-vetoed; it had nothing to do with Johnson's impeachment.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Party control alone was not the legal basis — the House needed a specific charge, which was the Tenure of Office Act violation.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Johnson was impeached for violating the Tenure of Office Act by dismissing Secretary of War Stanton without Senate consent.

items.stem: The party of this era that championed nativist policies was the

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1854 (Sarony & Co. lithograph; Library of Congress). Pre-1930 publication; PD tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: A. Free-Soil Party
B. Democratic Party
C. Know-Nothing Party
D. Whig Party
items.explanation: The Know-Nothing Party — officially the American Party — was the political expression of 1850s nativism. Alarmed by the surge of Irish and German Catholic immigrants, it demanded longer naturalization periods, restrictions on immigrant voting, and the exclusion of Catholics from office. No other party of the era made hostility to immigrants and Catholics its central platform.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Free-Soil Party organized against the expansion of slavery, not against immigrants.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Democrats of this era depended heavily on immigrant — especially Irish — votes and courted them, not attacked them.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Know-Nothing Party was the era's nativist party, built on anti-immigrant and anti-Catholic feeling.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Whigs were divided and collapsing in the 1850s; nativism found its home in the Know-Nothings, not the Whig platform.

items.stem: Radical Republicans favored all of the following EXCEPT
options: A. Military governance of the South
B. The impeachment of Andrew Johnson
C. Restoring ex-Confederate leaders to power
D. Electing newly enfranchised Black legislators
items.explanation: Radical Republicans demanded military rule in the South, pushed through Johnson's impeachment, and worked to elect newly enfranchised Black legislators. What they would never support was restoring ex-Confederate leaders to power — that was Andrew Johnson's lenient approach, which the Radicals fought. Returning the old planter leadership would have undone everything Reconstruction was meant to achieve.

option_explanations.A: Radicals did favor this, so it is not the answer. They divided the South into military districts under the Reconstruction Acts.
option_explanations.B: Radicals did favor this, so it is not the answer. They drove the impeachment of Andrew Johnson.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. Restoring ex-Confederate leaders was Johnson's policy, which Radical Republicans opposed; they wanted new Black and loyal-white leadership instead.
option_explanations.D: Radicals did favor this, so it is not the answer. They championed Black suffrage and the election of Black officeholders.

items.stem: Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the excerpt above?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Original diagram generated by the committed fixed-seed script gen_election_maps.py (this directory). No third-party source; electoral data cross-checked against published state-by-state results.
stimulus.text_stimulus: Paraphrased excerpt (facts and statistics only; not a quotation) — “1864: Lincoln v. McClellan,” Harpweek.com: About 78 percent of the Union electorate cast ballots in 1864. Lincoln won reelection in an Electoral College landslide, 212 votes to McClellan’s 21, and took about 55 percent of the popular vote — the third-largest share of the nineteenth century. McClellan carried only New Jersey, Delaware, and Kentucky. Lincoln’s coalition drew heavily on native-born farmers, skilled and professional workers, voters of New England descent, younger voters, and military personnel (he won an estimated 78 percent of the Union soldier and sailor vote); Democrats ran strongest in the cities and among Irish- and German-American voters. Republicans also widened their congressional majorities (149 to 42 in the House, 42 to 10 in the Senate), retook several state legislatures, and lost only the New Jersey governorship.

options: (A) Lincoln won the populous Northern states; McClellan carried sparser ones.
(B) Lincoln won the Election of 1864 because of Union successes during the Civil War.
(C) The Emancipation Proclamation mobilized Black voters in the South to vote for Lincoln in the Election of 1864.
(D) Republicans managed to gain control of Congress through the efforts of Lincoln to campaign on their behalf.
items.explanation: The 1864 electoral map shows Lincoln carrying the populous Northern states — with their large electoral vote totals — while McClellan won a scattering of less populous states. The pattern reflects the election's arithmetic: Lincoln's strength lay in the densely populated North, and that concentration of electoral votes decided the contest. The map's story is about where each candidate's votes were geographically concentrated.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The map shows Lincoln winning the populous Northern states with their big electoral hauls, while McClellan carried sparser, less populous ones.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The map shows geographic distribution of electoral votes, not the military causes of Lincoln's victory.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Black men could not vote in the South in 1864 — Southern states were in rebellion and the Fifteenth Amendment was years away.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The map concerns the presidential electoral vote, not congressional races or Lincoln's campaigning for Congress.

items.stem: According to the idea of Manifest Destiny,
options: A. Economics alone drove westward expansion
B. Politics alone drove westward expansion
C. Expansion fulfilled America's providential destiny
D. Eastern overpopulation forced expansion
items.explanation: Manifest Destiny was the belief that the United States was divinely ordained to spread across the North American continent. The word providential is the key: expansion was not just about economics, politics, or population pressure, but about fulfilling a destiny assigned by Providence. That sense of God-given mission is what made the idea so powerful in justifying territorial growth.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Economics mattered, but the doctrine's defining claim was providential destiny, not economics alone.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Politics mattered, but the doctrine's defining claim was providential destiny, not politics alone.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Manifest Destiny held that westward expansion fulfilled America's providential, God-given destiny.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Eastern overpopulation was not the doctrine's basis; the idea was about divine mission, not demographic pressure.

items.stem: The stated legal ground for Andrew Johnson's impeachment was

stimulus.pd_rationale: Published 1868 (Theodore R. Davis). Pre-1930 publication; Public Domain tag confirmed (observed 2026-10-01).

options: A. Violating the Tenure of Office Act
B. Violating the Reconstruction Act
C. Pursuing too lenient a Southern policy
D. Failing to enforce the Civil Rights Act of 1866
items.explanation: When the House drew up articles of impeachment against Andrew Johnson, the formal legal charge was his violation of the Tenure of Office Act — the 1867 law barring the president from removing Senate-confirmed officials without Senate approval. Johnson had fired Secretary of War Stanton in open defiance of the law. Whatever the political motives, the stated legal ground was that specific statutory violation.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The articles of impeachment charged Johnson with violating the Tenure of Office Act by removing Stanton.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Reconstruction Acts set up military rule in the South; they were not the law Johnson was charged with breaking.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Johnson's lenient Southern policy was the political background, but the legal ground stated in the articles was the Tenure of Office Act violation.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Civil Rights Act of 1866 was about citizenship and equal rights; it was not the statute named in the impeachment.

items.stem: The political logic of Johnson's veto is most similar to which twentieth-century position?
options: (A) Justice Murphy's dissent in Korematsu v. United States (1944).
(B) Joseph Welch's confrontation with McCarthy in the 1954 Army-McCarthy hearings.
(C) Governor Faubus's defiance of federal authority at Little Rock in 1957.
(D) John Lewis's support for the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
items.explanation: Andrew Johnson's vetoes of Reconstruction measures — such as the Freedmen's Bureau and Civil Rights bills — asserted that the federal government had no business overriding the states on matters of race and citizenship. That is the same structural logic as Governor Faubus's defiance at Little Rock in 1957: a state-level authority resisting federal power to preserve a racial order. Both positions pit state sovereignty against federal enforcement of Black rights.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Justice Murphy's Korematsu dissent defended civil liberties against the federal government — the opposite of Johnson's use of state power to limit Black rights.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Welch confronted McCarthy to defend the Army against anti-communist bullying, a different conflict about different principles.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Faubus's defiance of federal desegregation orders at Little Rock mirrors Johnson's vetoes: state authority invoked against federal power to resist Black civil rights.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. John Lewis supported federal action for voting rights — he stood with federal power, not against it.

items.stem: Which of the following was a significant political response in the 1850s to the development shown in the table?
options: (A) Congress enacted the National Origins quota system to cut off Irish immigration.
(B) Congress lengthened the naturalization waiting period to delay immigrant voting.
(C) President Pierce negotiated an immigration-limiting agreement with Ireland.
(D) The nativist Know-Nothing Party and its anti-immigrant, anti-Catholic platform.
items.explanation: The table shows the great wave of Irish immigration in the 1840s and 1850s, driven by the potato famine. The political response was the rise of the Know-Nothing Party, which turned anti-immigrant and anti-Catholic feeling into a national movement demanding restrictions on newcomers. Nativism became one of the most disruptive political forces of the decade.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The National Origins quota system was a 1920s policy, seventy years after the immigration wave shown in the table.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Congress did not lengthen the naturalization waiting period in the 1850s; the political response took the form of the Know-Nothing movement.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. President Pierce negotiated no immigration-limiting agreement with Ireland; the response was domestic and political.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The nativist Know-Nothing Party, with its anti-immigrant and anti-Catholic platform, was the decade's major political response to the immigration surge.

items.stem: The Grange emerged most directly in response to which nineteenth-century development?
options: (A) The wave of Irish immigration after the 1840s potato famine.
(B) The concentration of economic power in giant corporations.
(C) The rise of urban political machines.
(D) Corporate campaigns to control markets in Asia and Latin America.
items.explanation: The Grange — the Patrons of Husbandry, founded in 1867 — organized farmers who felt squeezed by railroad monopolies, grain-elevator operators, and banks that controlled the terms of rural economic life. Its cooperatives, lobbying, and Granger laws were a direct response to concentrated corporate power over farmers' livelihoods. The movement channeled agrarian anger at the middlemen and monopolies dominating the farm economy.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Irish immigration was an 1840s–1850s phenomenon; the Grange organized in the late 1860s around farmers' economic grievances.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Grange emerged to fight the railroads, grain monopolies, and banks whose concentrated power farmers blamed for their hardship.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Urban political machines were a city phenomenon; the Grange was a rural farm movement.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Campaigns to control Asian and Latin American markets were an imperial concern of the 1890s, not the cause of an 1860s farm organization.

items.stem: Nast's journalistic perspective is best compared to

stimulus.pd_rationale: Harper's Weekly, 1871-10-21 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 17–20 refer to the following cartoon.

[A Thomas Nast cartoon depicting Tammany Hall boss William M. Tweed as a bloated, grasping figure looming over New York City.]

options: A. Reporters investigating Nixon during Watergate
B. Muckrakers exposing Standard Oil
C. Yellow journalists of 1898
D. World War II correspondents
items.explanation: Thomas Nast's cartoons were investigative journalism in pictures: he spent years documenting and exposing the corruption of Boss Tweed's New York political machine with specific, evidence-based charges. That method — a sustained, documented investigation of a particular political scandal — most closely resembles the reporters who investigated Watergate, who likewise built a case against specific officials through painstaking evidence-gathering.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Like the Watergate reporters, Nast conducted a sustained investigation documenting a specific political corruption scandal — in his case, the Tweed Ring.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The muckrakers wrote broad exposés of industrial abuses like Standard Oil; Nast's work targeted one political machine's corruption, a narrower investigative campaign.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The yellow journalists of 1898 sensationalized foreign news to sell papers; Nast's cartoons were domestic political exposés built on documented charges.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. World War II correspondents reported from battlefields; Nast's journalism was the exposure of political corruption at home.

items.stem: Which of the following was most directly a cause of the success of the Populist Party?

stimulus.text: “We have witnessed for more than a quarter of a century the struggles of the two great political parties for power and plunder, while grievous wrongs have been inflicted upon the suffering people. We charge that the controlling influences dominating both these parties have permitted the existing dreadful conditions to develop without serious effort to prevent or restrain them. Neither do they now promise us any substantial reform. They have agreed together to ignore, in the coming campaign, every issue but one. They propose to drown the outcries of a plundered people with the uproar of a sham battle over the tariff, so that capitalists, corporations, national banks, rings, trusts, watered stock, the demonetization of silver and the oppressions of the usurers may all be lost sight of. They propose to sacrifice our homes, lives, and children on the altar of mammon; to destroy the multitude in order to secure corruption funds from the millionaires. “Assembled on the anniversary of the birthday of the nation, and filled with the spirit of the grand general and chief who established our independence, we seek to restore the government of the Republic to the hands of ‘the plain people,’ with which class it originated. We assert our purposes to be identical with the purposes of the National Constitution; to form a more perfect union and establish justice, insure domestic tranquility, provide for the common defence, promote the general welfare, and secure the blessings of liberty for ourselves and our posterity.” Source: Populist Party Platform, 1892

options: (A) Western farmers and ranchers favored conservation and organized to promote the National Parks system.
(B) The growth of corporate power and banking interests inspired rural activists to lobby for political reform.
(C) Western farmers resisted the mechanization of agriculture and resented government interference in rural affairs.
(D) After the Civil War, westward migration slowed, causing a long-term recession in many Western territories.
items.explanation: The 1892 Populist platform denounces capitalists, corporations, national banks, trusts, and the demonetization of silver — the forces farmers blamed for their suffering. The party succeeded because the growth of corporate and banking power gave rural activists a common enemy and a reform agenda: railroad regulation, silver coinage, and democratic reforms. Agrarian distress plus a clear corporate target turned protest into a political party.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Conservation and the National Parks were not the Populists' cause; their platform targeted banks, trusts, and the money supply.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The growth of corporate power and banking interests gave rural activists both their grievance and their reform program, driving the Populist Party's rise.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Farmers embraced mechanization; their complaint was about the economic power of railroads and banks, not government interference in rural affairs.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Westward migration continued after the Civil War, and the Populist surge came from economic grievance, not a migration slowdown.

items.stem: The popularity of such shows in the 1890s reflected

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1899 poster (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following poster.

[An 1890s Buffalo Bill's Wild West show poster depicts cowboys, Native American performers, and sharpshooters on horseback circling a stagecoach, beneath the banner 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West — Congress of Rough Riders of the World.']

options: A. Widespread opposition to immigration
B. The rise of the Populist Party in the 1890s
C. Eastern nostalgia for a 'vanishing' frontier
D. The discovery of gold in Alaska and the Yukon
items.explanation: In the 1890s, shows like Buffalo Bill's Wild West drew huge Eastern crowds with staged cowboys, Indians, and frontier drama. Their popularity reflected nostalgia: with the Census Bureau declaring the frontier closed in 1890, Easterners romanticized a West they believed was vanishing. The shows sold a mythic frontier to audiences who felt it slipping away.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Opposition to immigration was a nativist political current, not what drew crowds to Wild West entertainment.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Populist Party was a farmers' political movement; its rise does not explain the appeal of frontier spectacle.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Eastern audiences flocked to Wild West shows out of nostalgia for a frontier they believed was disappearing.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Alaska and Yukon gold discoveries came in 1896–1898 and involved a different frontier than the Wild West shows romanticized.

items.stem: The Anti-Saloon League succeeded where Nation's hatchet alone failed by

stimulus.text:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following quotation.

"I arrived at Wichita the 28th, the raid was postponed until the 29th. I took hatchets with me and we also supplied ourselves with rocks, meeting at the church, where we sang and prayed before smashing the saloon..."
—Carry A. Nation, on her saloon raids, 1900 (abridged)

options: A. Building a disciplined single-issue political lobby
B. Smashing more saloons than Nation
C. Opposing woman suffrage
D. Allying with the brewing industry
items.explanation: Carry Nation's hatchet raids were dramatic but scattered — smashing individual saloons changed no laws. The Anti-Saloon League succeeded by building something Nation never had: a disciplined, single-issue political lobby that graded candidates, mobilized voters, and pressured legislators in every state. Organization, not theatrics, is what carried Prohibition to the Eighteenth Amendment.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The League built a disciplined single-issue political machine that could reward friends and punish enemies at the ballot box — the organized pressure Nation's solo raids lacked.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Smashing more saloons was Nation's method; the League's innovation was political organization, not more destruction.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The League did not oppose woman suffrage; its focus was entirely on prohibition, and it often worked alongside suffragists.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The brewing industry was the League's mortal enemy, not its ally.

items.stem: A historian using this poster as evidence would most appropriately use it to study

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1899 poster (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 49–52 refer to the following poster.

[An 1890s Buffalo Bill's Wild West show poster depicts cowboys, Native American performers, and sharpshooters on horseback circling a stagecoach, beneath the banner 'Buffalo Bill's Wild West — Congress of Rough Riders of the World.']

options: A. The engineering of western railroads
B. The terms of Native American treaties
C. The actual wages paid to cowboys
D. Popular culture and western mythmaking
items.explanation: The poster's lurid imagery and exaggerated claims were designed to sell tickets and shape a romantic image of the West, not to record facts. A historian would use it to study how popular culture manufactured the western myth — the heroic cowboy, the lawless frontier — that shaped how Americans imagined the West. It is evidence of mythmaking, not of the realities it depicts.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. A promotional poster tells us nothing reliable about railroad engineering; it is advertising, not a technical document.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The poster is not a record of treaty terms; it is commercial imagery trading on frontier themes.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The poster's claims about pay are salesmanship, not payroll records — useless for studying actual wages.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The poster is best used to study popular culture and the mythmaking that created the romantic image of the West.

items.stem: The best evidence that working-class living standards improved in this era comes from
options: A. Comparing wage gains against rising living costs
B. Cataloging the new foods available in stores
C. Counting new amusement parks and theaters
D. Comparing immigrant wages with wages back home
items.explanation: The meaningful test of living standards is whether paychecks grew faster than the cost of living. Historians measure this by comparing wage gains against rising prices — real wages. If wages rose 20 percent while prices rose 10 percent, workers could buy more; if prices outpaced wages, they could buy less. Catalogs of new goods or amusement parks show what was available, not what workers could afford.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Comparing wage gains against rising living costs — real wages — is the direct measure of whether workers' purchasing power actually improved.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. New foods in stores show what existed, not whether working-class families could afford them.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Counting amusement parks shows leisure options existed, not whether workers had the money or time to enjoy them.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Comparing immigrant wages to wages back home measures the motive for immigration, not whether living standards rose over time in America.

items.stem: The above statements were most likely made after which major event?

stimulus.text: “Yesterday, December 7, 1941—a date which will live in infamy—the United States of America was suddenly and deliberately attacked by naval and air forces of the Empire of Japan. The United States was at peace with that nation and, at the solicitation of Japan, was still in conversation with its Government and its Emperor looking toward the maintenance of peace in the Pacific. Indeed, one hour after Japanese air squadrons had commenced bombing…the Japanese Ambassador to the United States and his colleague delivered to the Secretary of State a formal reply to a recent American message. While this reply stated that it seemed useless to continue the existing diplomatic negotiations, it contained no threat or hint of war or armed attack…. The attack yesterday…has caused severe damage to American naval and military forces. Very many American lives have been lost. In addition American ships have been reported torpedoed on the high seas…. As Commander-in-Chief of the Army and Navy, I have directed that all measures be taken for our defense.” Source: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, radio address, December 8, 1941

options: (A) The bombing of Pearl Harbor
(B) The sinking of the U.S.S. Maine
(C) The bombing of the U.S.S. Liberty
(D) The Boxer Rebellion
items.explanation: Roosevelt's address — a date which will live in infamy — was delivered to Congress on December 8, 1941, the morning after Japanese forces attacked Pearl Harbor. Every detail in the speech matches that event: the sudden naval and air attack, the severed diplomatic talks, the destroyed ships and lost lives. He spoke to ask Congress for a declaration of war.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The speech describes the December 7, 1941 Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor and was given the next day.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The U.S.S. Maine sank in Havana harbor in 1898, leading to the Spanish-American War — a different century and a different war.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The U.S.S. Liberty was attacked by Israel in 1967; it has no connection to this 1941 address.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Boxer Rebellion was the 1900 anti-foreign uprising in China, unrelated to Roosevelt's speech.

items.stem: Japanese-American internment began for all of the following reasons EXCEPT

stimulus.pd_rationale: U.S. War Relocation Authority photograph by Dorothea Lange, 1942-05-08 (U.S. federal work); Public domain tag on Commons; NARA record 537523.

options: A. Suspicions of divided loyalty in California
B. Press reports of Japanese-American sabotage
C. A need to protect Japanese Americans in camps
D. Racist portrayals in films and magazines
items.explanation: Japanese-American internment was driven by wartime suspicion of divided loyalty on the West Coast, press reports — largely false — of sabotage, and deep-seated racism amplified by films and magazines. Protection of Japanese Americans was not the reason: the camps were surrounded by barbed wire and guard towers, built to confine people, not shelter them. The policy was about fear and prejudice, not benevolence.

option_explanations.A: This did help cause internment, so it is not the answer. West Coast fears of divided loyalty fed the demand for removal.
option_explanations.B: This did help cause internment, so it is not the answer. Sensational press reports of sabotage — mostly unfounded — inflamed public opinion.
option_explanations.C: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. The camps were instruments of confinement driven by suspicion and racism, not a protective measure for Japanese Americans.
option_explanations.D: This did help cause internment, so it is not the answer. Racist portrayals in popular media reinforced support for removal.

items.stem: As a major part of the Treaty of Versailles, President Wilson sought to establish a League of Nations to

stimulus.text: “The Allied and Associated Governments affirm and Germany accepts the responsibility of Germany and her allies for causing all the loss and damage to which the Allied and Associated Governments and their nationals have been subjected as a consequence of the war imposed upon them by the aggression of Germany and her allies.” Source: The Treaty of Versailles, Article 231, 1919

options: (A) assemble an international forum for settling disputes through diplomacy and arbitration rather than war
(B) provide a stabilizing multinational security force to protect and defend international law
(C) counter future German aggression in Europe and Africa
(D) establish a common currency and international regulatory body for trade and economic growth
items.explanation: Wilson's central goal at Versailles was a League of Nations — a permanent international body where disputes could be settled through diplomacy, discussion, and arbitration instead of war. He believed a forum for collective deliberation would prevent future catastrophes like the one Europe had just endured. The League was meant to replace secret alliances and arms races with open negotiation.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Wilson sought the League as an international forum for settling disputes through diplomacy and arbitration rather than war.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Wilson envisioned deliberation and moral pressure, not a multinational standing army to enforce international law.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Countering Germany was the business of the treaty's punitive clauses; the League's purpose was forward-looking dispute resolution.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. A common currency and trade regulation were never part of Wilson's League proposal.

items.stem: Many senators opposed joining the League of Nations because

stimulus.pd_rationale: Punch (London) cartoon, 1919-12-01 (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons.

options: A. The U.S. would have to bankroll the League
B. The League could commit U.S. troops without Congress
C. The public unanimously opposed membership
D. Germany and Russia would dominate the League
items.explanation: The League's covenant — especially Article 10 — committed members to preserve each other's territorial integrity, which senators read as a promise to send American troops into foreign conflicts on the League's say-so. That struck at Congress's constitutional power to declare war. Led by Henry Cabot Lodge, opponents insisted the United States must never let an international body commit American forces without Congress's own decision.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Financing the League was not the core objection; the fight was about sovereignty and the war power.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Senators feared League membership could commit U.S. troops to foreign conflicts without a congressional declaration of war.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Public opinion was divided, not unanimously opposed; the Senate fight was led by senators with constitutional objections.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Germany was excluded from the League initially and Russia was in revolutionary turmoil; neither was poised to dominate it.

items.stem: In its Korematsu v. United States (1944) decision, the Supreme Court ruled that
options: (A) the wartime relocation of West Coast Japanese Americans was not unconstitutional
(B) the Japanese government had no legitimate claim to reparations for the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki
(C) the U.S. government had violated the Constitution by entering the Korean War
(D) immigration quotas based on race were unconstitutional
items.explanation: In Korematsu v. United States (1944), the Supreme Court upheld the wartime exclusion and relocation of Japanese Americans from the West Coast, ruling 6–3 that military necessity justified the policy. The Court held the relocation did not violate the Constitution. The decision has since become a symbol of how wartime fear can overwhelm civil liberties — and was effectively repudiated decades later.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The Court ruled that the wartime relocation of West Coast Japanese Americans was not unconstitutional.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The case concerned the relocation of Japanese Americans, not reparations for Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Korean War began in 1950, six years after this 1944 decision.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Race-based immigration quotas were not at issue in Korematsu; the case was about the wartime confinement of American residents.

items.stem: The cartoon reflects which continuity in American history?

stimulus.pd_rationale: 1899 photograph (pre-1930); Public domain tag on Commons; LOC print.

options: (A) Debates over whether constitutional rights should extend to the peoples of territories acquired by the United States
(B) Debates over the wisdom of asserting American control over foreign possessions
(C) Debates over the morality of U.S. tactics in colonial-independence wars
(D) Debates over permitting CIA covert operations abroad
items.explanation: The cartoon belongs to the long-running American debate over imperialism — whether the United States should assert control over foreign possessions like the Philippines, Puerto Rico, and Guam. That argument, fierce in 1898–1900, has recurred whenever America has taken or held overseas territory. The cartoon reflects the continuity of that debate across eras: expansionists celebrating new possessions, critics questioning the wisdom and cost of ruling them.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The cartoon addresses the broader wisdom of holding foreign possessions, not the specific constitutional question of rights in the territories.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The cartoon reflects the recurring debate over whether America should assert control over foreign possessions.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The cartoon is about the possession debate itself, not about the morality of military tactics in independence wars.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. CIA covert operations are a Cold War phenomenon, far removed from the imperialism debate the cartoon depicts.

items.stem: The United States became politically engaged with the Philippines after what military conflict?

stimulus.text: “The Opposition tells us that we ought not to govern a people without their consent. I answer, the rule of liberty that all just government derives its authority from the consent of the governed, applies only to those who are capable of self-government. We govern the Indians without their consent, we govern our territories without their consent, we govern our children without their consent. How do they know that our government would be without their consent? Would not the people of the Philippines prefer the just, human, civilizing government of this Republic to the savage, bloody rule of pillage and extortion from which we have rescued them? And, regardless of this formula of words made only for enlightened, self-governing people, do we owe no duty to the world? Shall we turn these peoples back to the reeking hands from which we have taken them? Shall we abandon them, with Germany, England, Japan, hungering for them? Shall we save them from those nations, to give them a self-rule of tragedy?…Then like men and not like children, let us on to our tasks, our mission, and our destiny.” Source: Albert J. Beveridge, “The March of the Flag,” 1898

options: (A) Mexican–American War
(B) World War II
(C) Spanish–American War
(D) The Boxer Rebellion
items.explanation: Albert Beveridge's 1898 speech celebrates American expansion and the taking of the Philippines — which the United States acquired from Spain in the Treaty of Paris ending the Spanish-American War. The war destroyed Spanish power in the Pacific, and the Philippines came to America as the prize. Beveridge's march of the flag is a direct celebration of that war's outcome.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The Mexican-American War (1846–1848) concerned the Southwest and California, not the Philippines.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. World War II came four decades after America first engaged with the Philippines.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The Spanish-American War of 1898 brought the Philippines under American control.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Boxer Rebellion (1900) was an anti-foreign uprising in China, unrelated to the Philippines.

items.stem: American rule in the Philippines led most directly to

stimulus.text:
Questions 41–44 refer to the following quotation.

"If England can govern foreign lands, so can America. If Germany can govern foreign lands, so can America. … Will you remember that we do but what our fathers did—we but pitch the tents of liberty farther westward, farther southward—we only continue the march of the flag?" —Albert Beveridge, "The March of the Flag," September 16, 1898 (abridged)

options: A. A bloody Filipino insurrection against American rule
B. Immediate Philippine independence
C. A Filipino-American alliance against Japan in 1899
D. The end of American naval power
items.explanation: Filipinos had been fighting Spain for independence and expected freedom when the Americans arrived; instead the United States annexed the islands. Emilio Aguinaldo's forces then turned their guns on the new occupier, and the result was the Philippine-American War of 1899–1902 — a brutal counterinsurgency that cost hundreds of thousands of Filipino lives. American rule began not with gratitude but with a bloody insurrection.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Annexation provoked a bloody Filipino insurrection against American rule — the Philippine-American War.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The United States annexed the Philippines rather than granting independence, which is precisely what sparked the fighting.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. There was no Filipino-American alliance against Japan in 1899; Filipinos were fighting the Americans themselves.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. American naval power was not ended; it was the instrument that made overseas empire possible.

items.stem: The Supreme Court decision above is best understood in the context of

stimulus.text: “We conclude that, in the field of public education, the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal. Therefore, we hold that the plaintiffs and others similarly situated for whom the actions have been brought are, by reason of the segregation complained of, deprived of the equal protection of the laws guaranteed by the Fourteenth Amendment.” Source: Brown v. Board of Education , 1954

options: (A) a resurgence of social conservatism in the wake of World War II
(B) an invigorated postwar economy as countries rebuilt after the war
(C) activists' postwar push for civil liberties at home after defeating tyranny abroad
