(D) a fear of communist government subversion in the wake of Stalinist expansion
items.explanation: Brown v. Board of Education (1954) struck down school segregation, and the decision belongs to the postwar civil rights surge. Black veterans had fought tyranny abroad in World War II and returned demanding democracy at home; the NAACP's legal campaign, the Double V spirit, and Cold War pressure to live up to American ideals all fueled the push. Brown was the legal climax of activists demanding that America match its wartime rhetoric with civil liberties for its own citizens.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The postwar years saw a civil rights advance, not a conservative resurgence — that came later, in the late 1960s and 1970s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Postwar prosperity was real, but it does not explain a school-desegregation ruling; the context was the fight for civil liberties.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Brown belongs to the postwar push by activists for civil liberties at home after America had defeated tyranny abroad.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Fear of communist subversion produced McCarthyism, not the desegregation of public schools.

items.stem: Ford's WIN program convinced many Americans that

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov}}: work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: A. He had no real grasp of economics
B. He brilliantly inspired the public
C. He lived in Nixon's shadow
D. He mastered foreign policy
items.explanation: President Ford's WIN campaign — Whip Inflation Now — asked Americans to wear WIN buttons and voluntarily cut spending to fight inflation. The gimmick struck most observers as embarrassingly unserious economics: inflation is a macroeconomic problem, not something button-wearing can fix. The program convinced many Americans that Ford had no real grasp of how the economy worked.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The WIN program's voluntary button-wearing approach to inflation convinced many that Ford had no real grasp of economics.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The program was widely mocked, not admired as brilliant inspiration.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Living in Nixon's shadow was a political problem for Ford, but WIN was judged on its economic merits — and found wanting.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Ford's foreign policy (détente, Helsinki) was separate; WIN was a domestic economic program.

items.stem: Which one of the following was a consequence of the liberal successes of the 1960s?

stimulus.text: “The challenge of the next half century is whether we have the wisdom to use wealth to enrich and elevate our national life, and to advance the quality of our American civilization…. The Great Society rests on abundance and liberty for all. It demands an end to poverty and racial injustice, to which we are totally committed in our time. But that is just the beginning. The Great Society is a place where every child can find knowledge to enrich his mind and to enlarge his talents. It is a place where leisure is a welcome chance to build and reflect, not a feared cause of boredom and restlessness. It is a place where the city of man serves not only the needs of the body and the demands of commerce but the desire for beauty and the hunger for community. It is a place where man can renew contact with nature. It is a place which honors creation for its own sake and for what it adds to the understanding of the race. It is a place where men are more concerned with the quality of their goals than the quantity of their goods. But most of all, the Great Society is not a safe harbor, a resting place, a final objective, a finished work. It is a challenge constantly renewed, beckoning us toward a destiny where the meaning of our lives matches the marvelous products of our labor.” Source: Lyndon Johnson, Remarks at the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, 1964

options: (A) Liberal Democrats abandoned antiwar protests in a show of support for President Johnson.
(B) Conservative Republicans mobilized to defend traditional mores and curb government authority.
(C) Economic recession was catalyzed by increased government spending, causing “stagflation.”
(D) A majority of Northern Black voters abandoned the Democratic Party, siding with Republicans.
items.explanation: The liberal triumphs of the 1960s — civil rights laws, Great Society programs, and court decisions expanding individual rights — provoked a powerful conservative backlash. Many Americans felt traditional values and local authority were under assault by an overreaching federal government. Conservative Republicans mobilized that resentment into a political movement to defend traditional mores and roll back government power — the backlash that carried Nixon and later Reagan.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Liberal Democrats split bitterly with Johnson over Vietnam; they did not rally behind him.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The 1960s liberal successes triggered a conservative mobilization to defend traditional values and curb federal authority.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Stagflation was a 1970s phenomenon with complex causes; it was not the direct political consequence of 1960s liberalism.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Northern Black voters remained overwhelmingly Democratic; they did not defect to the Republicans.

items.stem: The Korean War

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-Military-Marines}}: U.S. Marine Corps photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: (A) ended with the surrender of communist forces to the Americans in 1953
(B) resulted in substantial territorial gains for South Korea with respect to its prewar northern boundary
(C) demonstrated that the United States was reluctant to engage China in full-blown military conflict
(D) exemplified the willingness of the executive branch to defer to the military judgment of generals during wartime
items.explanation: The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice near the prewar border — no victory parade, no territorial gain. Its deeper significance was what America refused to do: despite General MacArthur's demands to strike China, Truman fired him and kept the war limited. The war showed the United States would fight communism but would not risk a full-scale war with China to win outright.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No communist surrender occurred; the war ended in a stalemate armistice, not a surrender.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The armistice line sat near the prewar 38th parallel; South Korea gained no substantial territory.
option_explanations.C: Correct. By refusing to expand the war into China and removing MacArthur, the United States showed its reluctance to engage China in full-blown conflict.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Truman's firing of MacArthur showed the executive asserting civilian control over the military, not deferring to generals.

items.stem: Which of the following groups would be most likely to support the point of view expressed by Kerry above?

stimulus.text: “We found that not only was it a civil war, an effort by a people who had for years been seeking their liberation from any colonial influence whatsoever, but also we found that the Vietnamese whom we had enthusiastically molded after our own image were hard put to take up the fight against the threat we were supposedly saving them from. “We found most people didn’t even know the difference between communism and democracy. They only wanted to work in rice paddies without helicopters strafing them and bombs with napalm burning their villages and tearing their country apart. They wanted everything to do with the war, particularly with this foreign presence of the United States of America, to leave them alone in peace, and they practiced the art of survival by siding with whichever military force was present at a particular time, be it Viet Cong, North Vietnamese or American.” Source: Statement by John Kerry of Vietnam Veterans Against the War

options: (A) A secretary of state in the 1820s enforcing the Monroe Doctrine
(B) A voter supportive of Manifest Destiny in the 1840s
(C) A journalist writing about the plight of Cubans in the 1890s
(D) A member of the Anti-Imperialist League in the 1900s
items.explanation: John Kerry testified that Vietnam was a civil war, that the Vietnamese wanted only to be left alone, and that American power was the foreign presence destroying their country. That is the classic anti-imperialist argument: a distant people fighting for self-determination against an outside empire. The Anti-Imperialist League of 1898–1900 made exactly that case against annexing the Philippines — that America was crushing another people's independence.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. An 1820s Monroe Doctrine enforcer asserted American dominance in the hemisphere — the opposite of Kerry's anti-intervention stance.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. A Manifest Destiny voter celebrated American expansion; Kerry condemned American intervention.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. A journalist on Cuban suffering in the 1890s might sympathize with victims, but the organized anti-imperialist position is the closer match.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Kerry's argument — that America was suppressing another people's liberation struggle — matches the Anti-Imperialist League's case against empire.

items.stem: Which of the following best reflects the spirit of the 1960 Democratic platform's 'New Frontier' proposals?

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-POTUS}}: official White House photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.
stimulus.text_stimulus:
Questions 11–12 refer to the following excerpt.

The 1960 Democratic platform called for a 'New Frontier' of expanded federal action: stronger support for education and health care, vigorous protection of civil rights, and renewed American leadership in science and space.
—After President John F. Kennedy, 'New Frontier' speech, 1960

options: A. Expanded federal efforts in education, health care, civil rights, and science
B. A return to 1920s laissez-faire economic policies
C. An isolationist withdrawal from international commitments
D. A rollback of New Deal-era federal programs in favor of state control
items.explanation: Kennedy's New Frontier promised active federal leadership: more money for education, expanded health care, stronger civil rights enforcement, and a dramatic commitment to science and space exploration. The platform rejected both laissez-faire retreat and isolationism. Its spirit was that energetic federal government could solve national problems — from classrooms to the moon.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The New Frontier called for expanded federal efforts in education, health care, civil rights, and science.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Kennedy rejected 1920s laissez-faire; the New Frontier meant more federal action, not less.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Kennedy was an internationalist — flexible response, the Peace Corps, the space race — not an isolationist.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The platform expanded the New Deal tradition of federal programs rather than rolling it back to the states.

items.stem: How did Depression and war shape the generation raising families in the 1950s?
options: A. They turned inward to family
B. They gave their children what they had lacked
C. They bought freely on credit
D. Both A and B
items.explanation: The generation that came of age in the Depression and World War II carried both experiences into parenthood. Having known scarcity and danger, they turned inward to the security of family life — and they were determined to give their children the stability, goods, and opportunities they themselves had lacked. Both impulses shaped the baby-boom household: the inward turn and the compensating generosity.

option_explanations.A: True, but incomplete on its own. The inward turn to family was real, yet so was the determination to provide more for children.
option_explanations.B: True, but incomplete on its own. Giving children what they had lacked was real, yet so was the inward turn to family.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This generation was famously cautious with money after the Depression; free spending on credit does not describe them.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Both A and B describe this generation: they turned inward to family and gave their children what scarcity had denied them.

items.stem: Which of the following happened during the 2000 presidential election?
options: (A) George W. Bush won the popular vote.
(B) Al Gore won the popular vote.
(C) The Supreme Court ordered a recount in Florida, after which Bush was declared the winner.
(D) The media prematurely declared Bush the winner, presumably causing voters who would have voted for Gore not to bother showing up at the polls.
items.explanation: In the 2000 election, Al Gore won the national popular vote by about half a million ballots, but the presidency turned on Florida's disputed electoral votes. After weeks of recount battles, the Supreme Court's Bush v. Gore decision ended the recount, and Florida — and the presidency — went to George W. Bush. The popular-vote winner lost the Electoral College.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Bush lost the popular vote; he won the presidency through the Electoral College.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Al Gore won the popular vote in 2000, though he lost the election.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Supreme Court halted the Florida recount rather than ordering one, and that halt secured Bush's victory.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Premature media calls were a feature of election night confusion, but the decisive fact was the popular-vote versus Electoral College split.

items.stem: For the U.S. military and the national defense industry, the consequences of the September 11 terrorist attacks did NOT include

stimulus.pd_rationale: Wikimedia Commons file page carries {{PD-USGov-Military-Air}}: U.S. Air Force photograph, a work of the U.S. federal government. Public domain.

options: (A) facing further large-scale attacks on U.S. soil
(B) the launch of two prolonged wars in the Middle East
(C) the establishment of the Department of Homeland Security
(D) a series of long-term investigations into the causes of the attack
items.explanation: The September 11 attacks did lead to two prolonged Middle East wars, the creation of the Department of Homeland Security, and long investigations into intelligence failures. What did not happen was another large-scale attack on American soil — the massive security overhaul that followed 9/11 succeeded, at least, in preventing a repeat of that scale. The homeland-security apparatus was built precisely to make sure it did not happen again.

option_explanations.A: Correct — this is the EXCEPT. No further large-scale attack on U.S. soil followed; preventing one was the point of the entire security response.
option_explanations.B: This did happen, so it is not the answer. The attacks led to the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.
option_explanations.C: This did happen, so it is not the answer. The Department of Homeland Security was created in 2002–2003.
option_explanations.D: This did happen, so it is not the answer. The 9/11 Commission and other inquiries investigated the attacks for years.

items.stem: The declaration's demands — worker and environmental protections in trade deals, and a democratic body accountable to citizens — best illustrate which of the following about the Seattle protests?

stimulus.text: A 1999 Global Exchange declaration, issued around the Seattle WTO protests, charged that the World Trade Organization was dominated by corporate interests and demanded trade policy representing all sectors of society, trade serving equitable and sustainable development with worker and environmental protections, and a democratic body accountable to citizens replacing the WTO. — paraphrased from Global Exchange (Seattle), 'Declaration for Global Democracy,' 1999

options: (A) They were organized and directed by the United States government.
(B) They united labor, environmental, and human-rights groups in a broad coalition.
(C) They endorsed corporate-led globalization as the path to prosperity.
(D) They demanded an end to all international trade.
items.explanation: The 1999 Seattle WTO protests were famous for the teamsters-and-turtles alliance: union members marching alongside environmentalists, with human-rights and community groups joining in. The Global Exchange declaration's demands — worker protections, environmental protections, democratic accountability — mirror exactly that coalition's shared agenda. The protests' defining feature was this broad, cross-movement coalition against corporate-led globalization.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The protests were directed against the WTO and U.S. trade policy, not organized by the government.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The Seattle protests united labor, environmental, and human-rights groups in a broad coalition, as the declaration's combined demands show.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The protesters opposed corporate-led globalization; they did not endorse it.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The declaration demanded fairer trade with protections, not an end to all international trade.

section_1b.directions: Section I, Part B — Short Answer: 3 questions, 40 minutes. Answer all three questions. Each question has three parts (A, B, C); write your answers in complete sentences. Question 1 is based on a secondary source, Question 2 on a primary source, and Question 3 on a non-text source (map, chart, image, or diagram). This part counts for 20 percent of the exam score.

questions.stimulus_text: Excerpt 1: Historian Andrew Hacker argues the Revolution cannot be understood apart from English imperial economic policy, which had aimed since Cromwell's era at protecting English capitalist interests. When colonial economic competition jeopardized those interests, London insisted only where fundamental mercantile principles were at stake. The struggle, in this view, was not truly about taxation powers or natural rights but about the survival of English mercantile capitalism within the imperial system. (Paraphrased from Andrew Hacker, The Triumph of American Capitalism, 1940.) Excerpt 2: Historian Bernard Bailyn argues that the language of 'slavery,' 'corruption,' and 'conspiracy' in Revolutionary writing was not mere propaganda. Used forcefully across social classes, positions, and denominations, these words reflected genuine fear and anxiety: colonists sincerely believed a comprehensive conspiracy against liberty — nourished by corruption, with American oppression its most visible part — lay at the heart of British policy. (Paraphrased from Bernard Bailyn, The Ideological Origins of the American Revolution, 1967.)
parts: Briefly describe ONE major difference between Hacker's and Bailyn's historical interpretations of the American Revolution.
Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development during the period 1754 to 1783 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Hacker's interpretation.
Briefly explain how ONE specific historical event or development during the period 1754 to 1783 that is not explicitly mentioned in the excerpts could be used to support Bailyn's interpretation.
exemplar: Hacker offers an economic interpretation: the Revolution was a struggle to preserve English mercantile capitalism against colonial competition, not a battle of constitutional ideas. Bailyn offers an ideological interpretation: colonists genuinely feared a deliberate conspiracy against liberty, and that fear — not economics — drove the Revolution.

Parliament's post-1763 revenue program — the Sugar Act (1764) and Stamp Act (1765), designed to make colonists pay for imperial defense and administration — supports Hacker's economic reading: the flashpoints were taxes and trade regulation protecting English commercial interests.

The colonial reaction to the Coercive Acts (1774) — widely read as proof that Parliament intended to enslave America, prompting the Continental Congress and extralegal committees — supports Bailyn: colonists acted on a sincere belief in an orchestrated conspiracy against their liberties.

questions.stimulus_text: "Since the peace was made [the 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne], you have kill'd some of the Shawanese, Winebagoes Delawares and Miamies and you have taken our lands from us and I do not see how we can remain at peace with you if you continue to do so. . . . We shall have a great council, at which all the tribes will be present, when we shall show to those who sold [land] that they had no right to [do so]. . . . If you will not give up the land and do cross the boundary of your present settlement, it will be very hard, and produce great troubles among us. . . . As we intend to hold our council at the Huron village, that is near the British, we may probably make them a visit. Should they offer us any presents of goods, we will not take them; but should they offer us powder and the tomahawk, we will take the powder and refuse the tomahawk." — Tecumseh, speech to Governor William Henry Harrison at Vincennes, Indiana Territory, 1810
parts: Briefly describe one likely purpose of Tecumseh in giving the speech.
Briefly explain how one historical development contributed to the circumstance discussed in the excerpt.
Briefly explain one development between 1810 and 1840 that resulted from situations such as the one depicted in the excerpt.
exemplar: Tecumseh aimed to convince Harrison that the Treaty of Fort Wayne was void — no single tribe's chiefs could sell land held in common — and to warn that if the United States kept seizing land, his united confederacy would resist by force and accept British military aid.

The 1809 Treaty of Fort Wayne, in which Harrison secured some three million acres from Delaware, Miami, and Potawatomi signers, created the crisis: Tecumseh insisted those chiefs had no authority to sell shared tribal territory, so settler occupation under the treaty was, to him, theft.

The confrontation fed directly into the War of 1812, when Tecumseh allied his confederacy with Britain against the United States; his death at the Thames in 1813 shattered pan-Indian resistance in the Old Northwest and cleared the way for further American expansion.

questions.stimulus_text: The 1777 engraving shows a peaceful commercial encounter: a European trader examines a beaver pelt offered by a Native American, while another Native man smokes a long pipe nearby and a second trader leans on a barrel of trade goods. The figures face each other calmly, conducting business as willing partners.
questions.attribution: Described from a 1777 engraving of fur traders in Canada.
parts: A. Briefly explain what the engraving suggests about the nature of early contact between Europeans and Native Americans.
B. Briefly explain how one detail of the image supports your answer to part A.
C. Briefly explain one longer-term effect of the type of contact shown on Native American societies in the period 1600 to 1750.
exemplar: The engraving suggests that early contact was cooperative and commercial, presenting Europeans and Native Americans as willing trading partners.
The trader examining the beaver pelt offered by the Native trader shows voluntary commercial exchange - business between willing partners - rather than conquest or coercion.
Participation in the fur trade drew Native societies into European market economies and rivalries, intensifying inter-tribal warfare over hunting grounds and access to European goods.

section_2a.directions: Section II, Part A — Document-Based Question: 1 question, 60 minutes (including a 15-minute reading period). The question is based on 7 documents. In your response you must develop a historically defensible thesis, describe a broader historical context, use at least 4 documents to support your argument, use at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents, and for at least 2 documents explain how the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, and/or audience is relevant to your argument. This part counts for 25 percent of the exam score.

dbq.prompt: To what extent did the Federalist administrations of George Washington and John Adams promote national unity and advance the authority of the federal government in the period 1789–1801?

documents.text: "I behold the surest pledges that … no local prejudices or attachments, no separate views or party animosities, will misdirect the comprehensive and equal eye which ought to watch over [Congress] … that the foundation of our national policy will be laid in the pure and immutable principles of private morality, and the preeminence of free government be exemplified by all the attributes which can win the affections of its citizens and command the respect of the world." —George Washington, First Inaugural Address (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Washington speaks as the unifying, above-party first president addressing Congress and the nation; his purpose is to legitimize the new federal government and bind diverse states to it. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalists promoted unity and federal authority—or, with Docs F/G, to show how far practice fell short of this ideal.

documents.text: "The General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Virginia … represent [that] … in an agricultural country like this … to perpetuate a large monied interest, is a measure which … must … produce … the prostration of agriculture at the feet of commerce, or a change in the present form of federal government, fatal to the existence of American liberty." —Virginia Resolutions on the Assumption of State Debts (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Virginia's legislature, led by opponents of Hamilton's financial program, protests to Congress; its purpose is to block assumption of state debts as unconstitutional and sectional. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist policies divided the nation along sectional lines and expanded federal power in ways critics called dangerous to liberty.

documents.text: "I consider the foundation of the Constitution as laid on this ground—that all powers not delegated to the United States, by the Constitution, nor prohibited by it to the states, are reserved to the states, or to the people. To take a single step beyond the boundaries thus specially drawn around the powers of Congress, is to take possession of a boundless field of power." —Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Jefferson writes privately to Washington as secretary of state, urging a veto; his purpose is to stop Hamilton's bank and defend strict construction. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist actions advanced federal authority beyond constitutional limits—or that even the administration's own cabinet saw its authority as overreach.

documents.text: "The powers contained in a constitution of government, especially those which concern the general administration of the affairs of a country, its finances, trade, defense, etc., ought to be construed liberally in advancement of the public good." —Alexander Hamilton, Opinion on the Constitutionality of the Bank (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Hamilton writes to Washington to justify the bank; his purpose is to establish the doctrine of implied powers and win presidential approval. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalists deliberately expanded federal authority—the clearest statement of the loose-construction doctrine that built national power.

documents.text: "Whereas combinations to defeat the execution of the laws laying duties upon spirits distilled within the United States … have … existed in some of the western parts of Pennsylvania; … it is in my judgement necessary … to take measures for calling forth the militia in order to suppress the combinations aforesaid, and to cause the laws to be duly executed." —George Washington, Proclamation on the Whiskey Rebellion (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Washington issues a presidential proclamation to the nation; his purpose is to justify using federal military force against domestic resistance and to demonstrate that federal law will be enforced. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalists decisively advanced federal authority—the first use of national military power to enforce a federal tax—though it also bred western resentment.

documents.text: "That if any person shall write, print, utter, or publish, any false, scandalous, and malicious writing … against the government of the United States … with the intent to defame the said government, … then such person … shall be punished by a fine not exceeding two thousand dollars, and by imprisonment not exceeding two years." —The Sedition Act (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: A Federalist Congress legislates during the Quasi-War crisis; its purpose is to silence Republican opposition press and critics of Adams. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist rule undermined national unity and abused federal authority—the strongest evidence that 'advancing authority' came at liberty's expense.

documents.text: "Resolved, that the several States … are not united on the principle of unlimited submission to their general government; … [the Sedition Act], which does abridge the freedom of the press, is not law but is altogether void." —Kentucky Resolutions (abridged)
documents.sourcing_note: POV/purpose: Kentucky's legislature, secretly drafted by Jefferson, answers the Alien and Sedition Acts; its purpose is to assert states' right to judge federal overreach and rally Republican resistance. Argument relevance: Use to argue Federalist policies fractured national unity, provoking the nullification doctrine that would haunt the republic for decades.

leq.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which reform movements played an important role in shaping American society from 1820 to 1860.
